title: Overview
text: Read this top to bottom once. Then keep it open while you build. Every section ends with the sentence you should be able to say in an interview. If you can't say it yet, that's the part to study.

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: Companies get **payment disputes**: a customer emails "I was charged twice", "my refund never came", "I don't recognise this charge". Someone has to read each one and put it in the right bucket (card networks like Visa and Mastercard define these buckets as *reason codes*). Wrong bucket means wrong evidence and a lost case.

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: You can automate that sorting four ways, each more sophisticated and more expensive than the last:

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: Rung: A · Approach: **Rules engine** · Plain English: A list of keyword patterns. "charged twice" → Duplicate. No AI.

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: Rung: B · Approach: **Single LLM call** · Plain English: Send the message + the 9 definitions to an AI model, get one answer.

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: Rung: C · Approach: **RAG** · Plain English: Same, but first *look up* the most relevant policy rules and give them to the model.

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: Rung: D · Approach: **Multi-agent** · Plain English: Three AI steps: propose an answer, verify it against policy, arbitrate if they disagree.

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: **Overkill measures all four on the same test set** and asks: *is each step up worth what it costs?* That's the whole project. The pipelines aren't the deliverable. **The comparison is.**

title: What is this project, in plain English?
text: "I'd start with the cheapest thing that could work, measure it against a labelled set, and only escalate where the error cost justifies it. I have the numbers from doing exactly that on dispute triage."

title: The map: how the pieces fit
text: Commands: data/eval.seed.jsonl ──┐ (180 disputes; becomes data/eval.jsonl after YOU relabel them) ; data/taxonomy.json ───┤ the 9 categories + definitions ; data/policy/*.md ─────┤ 46 policy documents (RAG reads these) ; ▼ ; pipelines/ rules.py single.py rag.py agents.py ← four implementations, ONE interface (base.py) ; llm.py (Groq client) retrieval.py (BM25 + vectors) graph.py (state machine) prompts.py ; │ each returns: label + token counts. Never cost or time. ; ▼ ; harness/ run.py times every call · prices every token (cost.py) · scores (score.py) ; │ checkpoints each case to runs/<pipeline>.jsonl ; ▼ ; results.json ───────► web/ (the dashboard, a static site you deploy on Vercel) ; ▲ ; serve.py local server: dashboard + live API (try any text against the real pipelines) ; mcp_server.py the same tools for Claude Desktop / Claude Code / any MCP client ; tools/label.py blind double-pa

title: The map: how the pieces fit
text: **Why one interface?** If every pipeline implements the same `classify(text) -> Result`, no pipeline can quietly get an easier job. **Why does the harness own timing and pricing?** A pipeline that reports its own latency can flatter itself. Ours can't: `harness/run.py` wraps every call in `time.perf_counter()` and prices the tokens the provider *reported*.

title: The map: how the pieces fit
text: Interview line: "Pipelines return token counts only; the harness owns timing and pricing. That's how I kept the benchmark from flattering any one approach."

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: Groq's free tier for `llama-3.3-70b-versatile` allows about **100,000 tokens per day** (TPD) and 1,000 requests per day (check yours at console.groq.com/settings/limits). Our estimates for the 180-case seed:

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: Pipeline: Single · Calls: 180 · Tokens: ~143k · Days on free tier: **~1.4 days** · Cost at list price: ~$0.09

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: Pipeline: RAG (k=3) · Calls: 180 · Tokens: ~219k · Days on free tier: **~2.2 days** · Cost at list price: ~$0.13

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: Pipeline: Agents · Calls: ~423 · Tokens: ~516k · Days on free tier: **~5.2 days** · Cost at list price: ~$0.31

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: At 420 cases, multiply by 2.3. That's about two weeks of free quota for everything. The harness handles this for you. It **stops cleanly** at the daily cap, **checkpoints** every case, and **resumes** next time you run the same command. Your options:

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: **Stay free (the plan):** run each pipeline a little every day; the harness resumes where it stopped. Tune on the dev split first (`--split dev`): it's 30% of the tokens, so most of your iterations fit in one day.

title: ⚠ The free-tier reality (read before you start)
text: Interview line: "The infra layer I built was the most useful part: backoff that honours retry-after, a client-side rate limiter, daily-cap detection, and per-case checkpointing. A crash at case 380 costs nothing, and re-running an unchanged pipeline costs nothing."

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: **What:** `data/eval.seed.jsonl` holds 180 disputes: 20 per category, mixed 40% clear / 35% paraphrase / 15% policy conflict / 10% stated-reason-wrong (exactly the runbook's mix).

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: **Honest status:** Claude drafted *and labelled* these as a seed. They're grounded in public card-network reason codes (Visa 10.4/12.x/13.x, Mastercard 48xx), but the labels are not yours yet. The dashboard shows a yellow "seed" banner until you fix that.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: Rewrite `data/taxonomy.json` definitions in your own words. Lock them.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: Read, edit and extend the disputes toward 420. Write new ones from consumer-complaint forums and network docs. Don't copy precedents from `data/policy/` (a test checks for leakage).

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: `python tools/label.py pass1` labels every case **blind** (you see text only).

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: **A day later:** `python tools/label.py pass2` (different order, blind to pass 1).

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: `python tools/label.py agree` gives your **self-agreement** and Cohen's kappa.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: `python tools/label.py resolve` settles each disagreement, or drops genuinely ambiguous cases.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: `python tools/label.py freeze` writes `data/eval.jsonl`. From then on it's frozen and the harness uses it.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: Re-run every pipeline (fingerprints change, so old rows are ignored automatically).

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: **Why blind and twice:** if you label after building pipelines you unconsciously write cases your pipelines pass, and the eval becomes a certificate instead of a measurement. Your self-agreement (say 96%) is the **ceiling**. No pipeline can meaningfully beat the consistency of its own labels. The dashboard draws it as a dashed line.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: **Dev/test split:** each case is assigned dev (30%) or test (70%) by a hash of its id (`harness/data.py`). You **tune** rules, prompts and k on dev, and **report** test. Tuning on the numbers you report is overfitting, and an interviewer will ask.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: **Confidence intervals:** with ~130 test cases, a 95% Wilson interval is about ±8 points. So "RAG 86% vs single 84%" is **noise**, not a finding. Say that before they do.

title: The eval set comes first, and it's labelled blind
text: Interview line: "I labelled before any pipeline existed, twice, a day apart. My self-agreement was X%, which is the ceiling. Differences under about 8 points on my test split are within the interval, so I don't claim them."

title: The difficulty tiers explain *why* each approach fails
text: Tier: clear · Example: "I was charged twice for the same order" · Who should win: everyone

title: The difficulty tiers explain *why* each approach fails
text: Tier: paraphrase · Example: "the café's ₹340 shows up two times, same timestamp" · Who should win: rules die here (no keyword)

title: The difficulty tiers explain *why* each approach fails
text: Tier: policy conflict · Example: "concert cancelled, organiser promised a refund, nothing came" (service? or credit?) · Who should win: **RAG**: precedence rule R2 decides

title: The difficulty tiers explain *why* each approach fails
text: Tier: stated reason wrong · Example: "Duplicate charge! My gym billed me again after I cancelled" · Who should win: **agents**: the verifier checks facts vs stated reason

title: The difficulty tiers explain *why* each approach fails
text: The 10 precedence rules in `data/policy/precedence.md` (R1–R10) are what make "policy conflict" cases decidable. Read them; you'll be asked to defend them.

title: Rung A: the rules engine (`pipelines/rules.py`, `rules.toml`)
text: Patterns are **regular expressions** per category, matched case-insensitively. **First match wins**, so order matters: most precise categories first.

title: Rung A: the rules engine (`pipelines/rules.py`, `rules.toml`)
text: **No match → human queue** (an abstention). It counts as *not correct* for accuracy, and lowers the **automation rate**. That's what a real rules engine does.

title: Rung A: the rules engine (`pipelines/rules.py`, `rules.toml`)
text: Patterns live in **TOML**, not Python. Python 3.11 reads TOML with the standard library (`tomllib`), so there's no YAML dependency. The file *is* the maintenance argument: someone edits it forever. That's why its fixed monthly cost ($400, an **assumption**) is the highest of the four.

title: Rung A: the rules engine (`pipelines/rules.py`, `rules.toml`)
text: The dashboard runs the **same rules.toml in your browser** (a test checks that JS and Python give identical labels on all 180 cases).

title: Rung A: the rules engine (`pipelines/rules.py`, `rules.toml`)
text: Interview line: "I tuned the rules properly, not as a straw man, on dev only, until it plateaued at X%. Rules match words; disputes are paraphrase. That's the ceiling, not lack of effort."

title: Rung B: one LLM call (`pipelines/single.py`, `prompts.py`)
text: Three things decide whether this lands near 87% or near 70%:

title: Rung B: one LLM call (`pipelines/single.py`, `prompts.py`)
text: **Forced output format:** we pass a *tool schema* whose `category` field is an **enum** of the 9 ids, and set `tool_choice` so the model *must* call it. No free-text parsing. Anything outside the enum is recorded as `parse_error`: **counted, never hidden or guessed**.

title: Rung B: one LLM call (`pipelines/single.py`, `prompts.py`)
text: **Definitions in the prompt**, not just names. The model can't tell "service not rendered" from "product not received" without them.

title: Rung B: one LLM call (`pipelines/single.py`, `prompts.py`)
text: **Zero-shot first.** Measure, then add few-shot examples and report the delta. The harness keeps every configuration in `history` (the "Tuning record" on the dashboard), so before/after is on record.

title: Rung B: one LLM call (`pipelines/single.py`, `prompts.py`)
text: **The gap between A and B is the most valuable number in the project.** It tells a client whether AI is worth starting at all. **Week-2 checkpoint:** if the gap is under 10 points, your eval set is too easy. Add harder paraphrase cases before building anything else. The dashboard warns you automatically.

title: Tokens, cost and latency (`harness/cost.py`, `harness/score.py`)
text: **Tokens:** the provider reports `prompt_tokens` and `completion_tokens` for every call. We sum them per case. The tool schema also counts as prompt tokens, which is why prompts look "bigger" than their text.

title: Tokens, cost and latency (`harness/cost.py`, `harness/score.py`)
text: **Price:** $0.59 per 1M input tokens and $0.79 per 1M output tokens (read 2026-11-06; confirm on groq.com/pricing). The free tier bills $0, but we **price at list price** so the comparison shows production cost.

title: Tokens, cost and latency (`harness/cost.py`, `harness/score.py`)
text: **Cost per 1k disputes** = average cost per case × 1,000. Small numbers, big volumes.

title: Tokens, cost and latency (`harness/cost.py`, `harness/score.py`)
text: **Latency:** p50 (median) and **p95** (95% of calls are faster than this). The first 5 calls of each session are discarded as warm-up.

title: Tokens, cost and latency (`harness/cost.py`, `harness/score.py`)
text: Interview line: "Mean latency hides the tail, and the tail is what breaks an SLA."

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation:** search a document store for the most relevant passages, put them in the prompt, then generate.

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **Corpus:** 46 short documents: per category a definition with qualifying conditions, an evidence and exclusions doc, and two worked precedents, plus the 10 precedence rules. A thin corpus makes RAG score the same as a single call. That's a failed *corpus*, not a failed pipeline.

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **Chunk by document, not by token count.** Each `## section` is one coherent rule (60–150 words). Fixed 512-token chunks would cut conditions away from the rule they qualify. *Say why you didn't chunk by token count; that answer distinguishes you.*

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **BM25** is classic keyword scoring (term frequency × rarity, with length normalisation). Written in about 30 lines of Python, it catches exact terms like "chargeback", amounts and merchant names.

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **Embeddings** turn text into vectors; similar meaning → nearby vectors (cosine similarity). We use `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` locally via `fastembed` (free, CPU, no torch). Don't swap embedding models; it's a rabbit hole with small returns.

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **pgvector** is a Postgres extension that stores vectors and searches them with SQL (`<=>` is the cosine distance operator). Setup: create a free Supabase project, enable the `vector` extension, put `DATABASE_URL` in `.env`, then run `python tools/ingest_pgvector.py`. No index on purpose: at 46 rows an exact scan is exact and faster (add HNSW past ~10k rows).

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **Hybrid search** = run both, combine with **Reciprocal Rank Fusion**: `score = Σ 1/(60 + rank)`. Without fastembed installed, RAG runs BM25-only and **results.json records that**.

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **Tune in this order, on dev, measuring after each:** k ∈ {1, 3, 5, 8} (there's a peak, then more context distracts) → hybrid vs BM25-only → reranking (cut first if short on time). Set k with `RAG_K=5 python run_eval.py -p rag --split dev`.

title: Rung C: RAG (`pipelines/rag.py`, `retrieval.py`)
text: **Retrieval attribution:** for every wrong answer we check whether any retrieved doc spoke about the correct category. *Retrieval missed* (fix: search) vs *model ignored good context* (fix: prompt). The dashboard shows both counts. Almost nobody separates these.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: Commands: START → classifier ─ok→ verifier ─accept→ END ; │ └─reject→ arbiter → END (label, or human_review) ; └─unparsed→ END (human_review)

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Classifier:** RAG plus a `runner_up` and a confidence.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Verifier:** fetches the policy *for the proposed category only* and checks its qualifying conditions. It can **reject**, naming the failed condition and the category policy points to.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Arbiter:** runs **only when the verifier rejects**. That conditional edge is the whole design. An unconditional three-call chain is a long prompt, not a multi-agent system, and costs roughly 40% more.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Human review is a real outcome.** If the arbiter can't decide, or its confidence is below τ=0.6 (`AGENT_HUMAN_THRESHOLD`), the case goes to a human. We count **resolved automatically / routed to human / wrong** separately. *Automation rate* is the number an operations leader cares about.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Why our own 40-line graph instead of LangGraph?** Three nodes and one conditional edge don't need a framework (CLAUDE.md rule). `graph.py` mirrors LangGraph's API exactly (`add_node`, `add_edge`, `add_conditional_edges`, `compile`, `invoke`), so switching is one import: `from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END`. Being able to explain both is the senior answer.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Verbalised confidence is poorly calibrated.** That's why the verifier exists: it checks *facts*, not the model's opinion of itself.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: **Tracing:** every step (node, tokens, verdict, docs) is stored in `runs/agents.jsonl` and drawn on the dashboard. Add `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`/`SECRET_KEY` to `.env` for hosted waterfalls in Langfuse Cloud (free). Export happens *after* the timed region, so upload time never counts as latency. ⚠ The Langfuse exporter uses their public ingestion API and is untested against a live account; check one trace after your first run.

title: Rung D: multi-agent (`pipelines/agents.py`, `graph.py`)
text: The finding to expect (and say plainly): "Agents bought ~1–2 points over RAG for several times the token spend and roughly 4× the latency. Here is the volume and error-cost combination where that's worth it."

title: The cost model: where the money conversation happens
text: Section "What it costs to be right" on the dashboard:

title: The cost model: where the money conversation happens
text: Commands: monthly cost = fixed infra + volume × (token cost per case ; + wrong-rate × cost of a wrong auto-decision ; + abstain-rate × cost of a human review)

title: The cost model: where the money conversation happens
text: Accuracy, abstention and tokens are **measured**. Fixed infra is an **assumption** (each pipeline states its basis; change them in the pipeline classes). Error and review costs are **the client's numbers**. Move the sliders, switch to ₹ (lakh/crore ticks), read the break-even points. At high error cost, accuracy wins. At low volume, fixed cost wins. That's the trade-off you sell.

title: Autopilot: the "computer use" button
text: Flip **Autopilot** in the top bar and the agent takes the mouse. A cursor moves across the console: it opens disputes from the inbox, types them into the workbench, **finds** relevant policy (BM25 in the browser), runs all four pipelines, follows the agent graph's path, decides, and **files** each case into the Outbox (auto-resolved / human review / mismatch). Then you export the triage as CSV or JSON. With `serve.py` running, filed cases are also written to `outbox/triage-<date>.jsonl` on disk.

title: Autopilot: the "computer use" button
text: Two missions: **triage the inbox** (one case per difficulty tier) and **hunt failure modes** (finds cases where pipelines disagree with the label or with each other, and explains which rule fired). Esc or the toggle gives control back. On wide screens the log docks on the right so it never covers what the agent is clicking.

title: Autopilot: the "computer use" button
text: **What it is and isn't:** it operates *this console*, using real pipelines (live via `serve.py` + key) or their recorded runs. It doesn't control your operating system. For true desktop computer use, connect `mcp_server.py` to an agent that has computer-use tools (next section). Then that agent can call `classify_dispute`, `search_policy`, `get_results` and `get_case` as tools.

title: MCP: plugging Overkill into any AI assistant
text: **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** is a standard way for AI apps to call external tools. Our `mcp_server.py` speaks it over stdin/stdout as JSON-RPC 2.0 (`initialize` → `tools/list` → `tools/call`), using only the standard library, so you can read every line of the protocol.

title: MCP: plugging Overkill into any AI assistant
text: Commands: claude mcp add overkill -- python /absolute/path/to/overkill/mcp_server.py # Claude Code

title: MCP: plugging Overkill into any AI assistant
text: Commands: {"mcpServers": {"overkill": {"command": "python", "args": ["/absolute/path/to/overkill/mcp_server.py"]}}}

title: MCP: plugging Overkill into any AI assistant
text: Claude Desktop → `claude_desktop_config.json`: Then ask: *"Use overkill to classify: 'I paid the plumber by transfer and he charged my card too'"* or *"Summarise the overkill results and tell me which pipeline a 50k/month client should use."*

title: New in v0.2: critic, red team, cascade, themes, tutorial
text: **The skeptical reviewer** (dashboard section *Critic*): every check an interviewer would run, computed live from results.json, with an interview-readiness score. Seed labels = FAIL; overlapping intervals = "inside the noise"; tiny tiers, dev≫test, partial/stale runs, parse errors, stale prices. Fix the reds before quoting numbers.

title: New in v0.2: critic, red team, cascade, themes, tutorial
text: **⚡ Red-team it** (console): attacks the current dispute with 8 rewrites (typo storm, Hinglish code-mix, keyword-free rewording, SMS-speak, ALL-CAPS rage, buried in small talk, wrong stated reason, ten words) and shows which pipeline breaks. Rules run in-browser; with `serve.py` + key the single call is attacked too. **Export as eval drafts** downloads the rewrites *unlabelled*: label them blind before adding them to the set. Autopilot red-teams one paraphrase case per mission.

title: New in v0.2: critic, red team, cascade, themes, tutorial
text: **E · Cascade** (`pipelines/cascade.py`): `llama-3.1-8b-instant` answers first; below `CASCADE_THRESHOLD` confidence it escalates to the 70B + RAG. This is the cheapest agentic routing pattern. It mixes models, so it is marked `comparable=false` and shown *beside* the ladder, never on it (the CLAUDE.md exception). Each model is priced at its own rate ($0.05/$0.08 per 1M for the 8B). Tune the threshold on dev: small-model confidence is poorly calibrated. The question it answers: what share escalates, and does accuracy survive?

title: New in v0.2: critic, red team, cascade, themes, tutorial
text: **Five themes:** Daylight, Midnight, Aurora, Terminal, Paper (press **T** to cycle). Data colours keep the validated ramp of the theme's light/dark mode; themes only restyle surfaces, ink and type.

title: New in v0.2: critic, red team, cascade, themes, tutorial
text: **Tutorial** (`web/tutorial.html`): eight chapters with commands, "check yourself" questions and saved progress.

title: Your next five weeks
text: **Deploy (Vercel, free):** import the GitHub repo into Vercel → set **Root Directory** to `overkill/web` → Framework: *Other* → Deploy. `run_eval.py` re-publishes `web/` after every run, so commit and push to update the live page. It's static, so it's never "down" when a recruiter opens it.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Why test rules first?** Cheapest thing that could work; it sets the floor that gives every other number meaning.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **How do I know your labels are right?** Blind, twice, a day apart, self-agreement X%; disagreements resolved by policy or dropped.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Did you tune on your test set?** No: a hash-based dev/test split; tuning on dev, reporting test.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Is 86 vs 84 a real difference?** At n≈130 the 95% interval is about ±8 pts; no. Here's what *is* significant…

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Why chunk by document?** Each rule is a coherent unit; token chunks split conditions from their rule.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Why hybrid search?** Disputes contain exact terms (amounts, "chargeback") that BM25 catches and embeddings blur.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **When RAG was wrong, why?** Retrieval missed N times, model ignored good context M times: different fixes.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Why not Qdrant or Pinecone?** One vector store; pgvector lives in the Postgres I already have. A second store adds a logo and subtracts credibility.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Is your multi-agent system just a chain?** No: the arbiter only runs on rejection (conditional edge); that's ~40% cheaper than an unconditional chain.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **Why not LangGraph?** Three nodes don't need a framework; my graph mirrors its API, so it's a one-line swap when I need checkpointing.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **How did you handle rate limits?** Client-side limiter, backoff honouring retry-after, daily-cap detection, checkpoint/resume.

title: Interview questions you will get (fill in your numbers)
text: **What would you build for us?** The sentence in section 0, plus the cost model with *their* volume and error cost.

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: Sell **the method, not the tool**. Nobody buys a dispute benchmark. People pay for the answer to *"are we about to overspend on AI, and how would we know?"* Overkill is your proof you can answer it.

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: **How this repo becomes a client deliverable (2 weeks):**

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: Replace `data/taxonomy.json` + `data/policy/` with *their* categories and policy (support tickets, KYC flags, lead routing: any classification task).

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: Build 100–200 labelled cases with their team using `tools/label.py` (their people label blind, so self-agreement is measured on *their* data).

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: Run the rungs cheapest-first with `run_eval.py`.

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: Set the cost model to their volume, error cost and review cost (₹ toggle), and read the break-even.

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: Deploy their dashboard (Vercel, free) as the live artifact for their CFO. Add a one-page recommendation.

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: **Pricing anchors (from your runbook; test them, don't trust them):** first two engagements ₹20k–30k for a named testimonial; after two case studies ₹60k–1.2L per review; optional oversight ₹25k–40k/month, capped at 3 months. Anchor the price against the overbuild you prevent, not your hours.

title: Turning this into money (an *AI Build Decision Review*)
text: **Before taking money:** read your internship agreement's outside-work and IP clauses (you said you've checked; keep it in writing). Keep Overkill free of any employer data, code or time. In every engagement note, state plainly that you measure and recommend; you don't guarantee production accuracy.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: Dashboard says "couldn't load data files" · Fix: You opened `index.html` as a file. Run `python serve.py`.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: `GROQ_API_KEY is not set` · Fix: `cp .env.example .env`, paste the key

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: Run stops with "daily limit reached" · Fix: Expected on the free tier. Run the same command tomorrow; it resumes.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: RAG says `mode: bm25` · Fix: `pip install fastembed` for hybrid (first run downloads ~70 MB of model)

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: `results.json` shows "stale" · Fix: You changed the eval set. Re-run each pipeline.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: Tests fail after editing policy docs · Fix: A precedent may share 7+ words with an eval case (leakage test). Reword it.

title: Troubleshooting
text: Symptom: Want to re-run from scratch · Fix: `--fresh` ignores checkpoints (costs tokens again)

title: Glossary
text: **Abstain:** the system declines to decide and routes to a human.

title: Glossary
text: **Automation rate:** share decided without a human.

title: Glossary
text: **BM25:** keyword relevance scoring.

title: Glossary
text: **Checkpoint:** saving progress per case.

title: Glossary
text: **Confusion matrix:** true category (rows) vs predicted (columns).

title: Glossary
text: **Embedding:** a vector representing meaning.

title: Glossary
text: **Fingerprint:** hash of a pipeline's config; changes invalidate old results.

title: Glossary
text: **Few-shot:** examples in the prompt.

title: Glossary
text: **MCP:** Model Context Protocol, a standard for AI tool calling.

title: Glossary
text: **p95:** the latency 95% of calls beat.

title: Glossary
text: **pgvector:** vectors inside Postgres.

title: Glossary
text: **RAG:** retrieve, then generate.

title: Glossary
text: **RRF:** Reciprocal Rank Fusion.

title: Glossary
text: **Self-agreement:** how often your two blind labelling passes agree.

title: Glossary
text: **TPD/RPD/TPM/RPM:** tokens/requests per day/minute.

title: Glossary
text: **Wilson interval:** an honest confidence interval for a proportion at small n.
